Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or SHA1 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or MD5 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or SHA1 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or MD5 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45659")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45659")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Fission Environment CRD create/update with dangerous SecurityContext on standalone container (CVE-2026-50566) AIExploitation High
Hunts Kubernetes API audit events where a Fission Environment CRD (apiGroup fission.io) is created/updated carrying privileged, allowPrivilegeEscalation, or dangerous-capability SecurityContext specifically on the standalone spec.runtime.container / spec.builder.container fields — the exact field the round-4 PodSpec sanitiser missed. This is the earliest and highest-fidelity catch of the CVE-2026-50566 admission bypass before any pod is scheduled. Rationale: Pivots on the exact article strings: objectRef.resource=environments + apiGroup fission.io, and the standalone spec.runtime.container/spec.builder.container securityContext fields with privileged/allowPrivilegeEscalation/SYS_ADMIN/NET_ADMIN/SYS_PTRACE — the precise merge-layer gap named in the advisory PoC. Defender/Falcon/CloudTrail left empty because K8s API audit telemetry is not in those schemas. Corroborated against NVD and GitLab/CIRCL advisories. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m63v-2g9w-2w6v • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-50566 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/fission/fission/CVE-2026-50566/

Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cluster administrator deliberately creating a debug/system Fission Environment with elevated capabilities (should be rare and reviewed)
  • GitOps controller (ArgoCD/Flux) reconciling an Environment manifest that legitimately declares NET_ADMIN for a networking function
  • Fission upgrade/CI tooling re-applying pre-existing environment definitions
  • Security team re-running the CVE-2026-50566 PoC during patch validation
  • A pre-existing (pre-patch) privileged environment being updated for an unrelated field, re-emitting the SecurityContext
Suppression filter
| where Actor !startswith "system:serviceaccount:argocd:" and Actor !startswith "system:serviceaccount:flux-system:" and Actor !endswith ":cluster-admin"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the Username/service account and sourceIPs on the audit event; confirm it is a tenant (not cluster-admin) principal and check whether the Environment name/namespace is expected. Verify cluster Fission version < 1.24.0 (vulnerable). 2) CONTAIN: Delete or revert the offending Environment CRD; revoke environments.fission.io create/update RBAC from the identity; apply a Kyverno/OPA policy rejecting dangerous container SecurityContext and label the function/builder namespace pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all pods in fission function/builder namespaces for privileged/added-capability containers (UC2); review audit logs from the same principal for exec/attach into resulting pods, node filesystem access, and secret reads indicating a completed escape.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where tostring(ObjectRef.resource) == "environments" and tostring(ObjectRef.apiGroup) == "fission.io"
| extend RuntimeSC = RequestObject.spec.runtime.container.securityContext
| extend BuilderSC = RequestObject.spec.builder.container.securityContext
| where tostring(RuntimeSC.privileged) == "true"
    or tostring(BuilderSC.privileged) == "true"
    or tostring(RuntimeSC.allowPrivilegeEscalation) == "true"

    or tostring(BuilderSC.capabilities.add) has_any ("SYS_ADMIN","NET_ADMIN","SYS_PTRACE")
| project TimeGenerated, Verb, Actor = Username, Namespace = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), EnvName = tostring(ObjectRef.name), RuntimeSC, BuilderSC, UserAgent, SourceIPs = RequestObject.spec
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Fission Environment CRD Privileged Standalone Container SecurityContext (CVE-2026-50566)
id: 6f3b1c8a-2d4e-4a91-9b7c-8e1a2f5c9d20
description: Detects create/update of a Fission Environment CRD whose standalone runtime.container or builder.container SecurityContext requests privileged, allowPrivilegeEscalation, or dangerous Linux capabilities, bypassing the PodSpec-only admission validation.

  selection_bpriv:

index=* sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" (verb=create OR verb=update OR verb=patch) objectRef.resource=environments objectRef.apiGroup=fission.io

Privileged / dangerous-capability pod scheduled in Fission function/builder namespace by executor SA AIInstallation Medium
Defence-in-depth for CVE-2026-50566: catches the resulting pod when the Fission executor/buildermgr service account schedules a pod containing a privileged, allowPrivilegeEscalation, or dangerous-capability container. Fires even if a future variant uses a different bypass field, because it inspects the actual materialised Pod SecurityContext rather than the Environment CRD. Rationale: Targets the materialised outcome described in the impact section: a privileged/dangerous-capability container scheduled under the executor's high-privilege service account (system:serviceaccount:fission*) or bearing the fission environmentName label. Complements UC1 by inspecting the Pod SecurityContext directly, so it survives field-name variants of the bypass. K8s-audit-only telemetry, hence Defender/Falcon/CloudTrail empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m63v-2g9w-2w6v • https://www.thehackerwire.com/fission-critical-container-escape-and-privilege-escalation-cve-2026-50566/
ATT&CKT1610 T1611
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately privileged Fission system component if the operator intentionally runs one (verify against Fission Helm values)
  • Node-level DaemonSets sharing the fission namespace that legitimately require NET_ADMIN
  • Third-party admission mutating webhook injecting a privileged sidecar into fission pods
  • Migration/upgrade jobs run by the fission executor SA during a version bump
  • Cluster monitoring agent pod co-scheduled in the fission namespace with SYS_PTRACE for profiling
Suppression filter
| where ContainerName !in ("fission-fetcher") and PodGenerateName !startswith "fission-upgrade"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the pod's ownerReference/environmentName label ties it to a Fission Environment, and cross-reference UC1 to see which Environment CRD produced it; note the executor SA and namespace. 2) CONTAIN: Delete the pod and its parent Environment/Deployment; cordon the node it landed on and inspect for host mount or hostPID/hostNetwork abuse; rotate any secrets reachable from that namespace. 3) HUNT: kubectl-audit for exec/attach into the pod, and check node auditd/EDR for container-escape indicators (writes to /proc, host filesystem access, nsenter). Sweep all fission namespaces for other privileged pods and enumerate identities holding environments.fission.io create/update RBAC.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb == "create" and tostring(ObjectRef.resource) == "pods"
| where Username startswith "system:serviceaccount:fission" or isnotempty(tostring(RequestObject.metadata.labels.environmentName))
| mv-expand Container = RequestObject.spec.containers
| extend SC = Container.securityContext
| where tostring(SC.privileged) == "true"
    or tostring(SC.allowPrivilegeEscalation) == "true"
    or tostring(SC.capabilities.add) has_any ("SYS_ADMIN","NET_ADMIN","SYS_PTRACE")
| project TimeGenerated, ExecutorSA = Username, Namespace = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), PodGenerateName = tostring(RequestObject.metadata.generateName), EnvLabel = tostring(RequestObject.metadata.labels.environmentName), ContainerName = tostring(Container.name), SC
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:create @objectRef.resource:pods (@user.username:system\:serviceaccount\:fission* OR @requestObject.metadata.labels.environmentName:*) (@requestObject.spec.containers.securityContext.privileged:true OR @requestObject.spec.containers.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation:true OR @requestObject.spec.containers.securityContext.capabilities.add:(SYS_ADMIN OR NET_ADMIN OR SYS_PTRACE))
CLOUD
index=* sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" verb=create objectRef.resource=pods
| spath output=fissionEnv path=requestObject.metadata.labels.environmentName
| spath output=fissionUid path=requestObject.metadata.labels{}
| search (user.username="system:serviceaccount:fission*" OR fissionEnv=*)
| spath output=priv path=requestObject.spec.containers{}.securityContext.privileged
| spath output=ape path=requestObject.spec.containers{}.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation
| spath output=caps path=requestObject.spec.containers{}.securityContext.capabilities.add{}
| where priv="true" OR ape="true" OR match(caps,"SYS_ADMIN|NET_ADMIN|SYS_PTRACE")
| table _time user.username objectRef.namespace requestObject.metadata.generateName fissionEnv priv ape caps
| sort - _time

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CISA KEV: CVE-2026-48558 — SimpleHelp Authentication Bypass Vulnerability

CISA KEV
2026-06-29 1 use case 0 techniques 2 kill-chain phases detected

SimpleHelp contains an authentication bypass vulnerability in the OIDC authentication flow. When OIDC authentication is configured, identity tokens submitted during login are accepted without verifying their cryptographic signature. In a vulnerable configuration, a remote, unauthenticated attacker can submit a forged token containing arbitrary identity claims to obtain a fully authenticated technician session. In some configurations, this may also allow bypass of multi-factor authentication. Vendor: SimpleHelp , Product: SimpleHelp. Federal patch due: 2026-07-02.

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Threat Brief: Mitigating Large-Scale Credential Attacks

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-06-26 11 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

We provide guidance for preparing for and mitigating large-scale credential attacks, focusing on recent campaigns targeting security vendors' devices. The post Threat Brief: Mitigating Large-Scale Credential Attacks appeared first on Unit 42 .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] FortiBleed password-spray success burst against internet-facing Fortinet/edge auth · [LLM] FortiGate jsconsole / loopback admin login (CVE-2024-55591 auth-bypass exploitation) · [LLM] FortiBleed MSSQL login-failure burst then success (internet-exposed SQL spraying) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] FortiGate rogue super_admin / SSL-VPN account creation following CVE-2024-55591 exploit · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
FortiBleed password-spray success burst against internet-facing Fortinet/edge auth AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a single source IP producing a high volume of failed authentications against a Fortinet appliance (SSL-VPN / admin login) followed by a successful login in the same window — the exact 'successful logins shortly after large-volume password failure events' pattern Unit 42 flags for the FortiBleed credential-spraying campaign. Rationale: Implements Unit 42's explicit FortiBleed guidance — audit remote-access logs for successful logins shortly after large-volume failure events — scoped to Fortinet auth via the CIM app values / DeviceVendor='Fortinet'. Threshold + same-window success join is what separates spray-then-compromise from routine VPN typos. Cross-checked with SOCRadar/SecurityWeek FortiBleed reporting and Arctic Wolf's CVE-2024-55591 analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/what-is-fortibleed/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/ • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1110.004 T1133
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote worker repeatedly fat-fingering an SSL-VPN password then succeeding
  • Misconfigured VPN client or saved-credential loop retrying stale creds before a successful re-auth
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanner (Qualys/Tenable) credential checks against the appliance
  • Shared NAT egress IP where many staff log in (inflated failure+success counts from one SourceIP)
  • Password-rotation day causing widespread first-attempt failures followed by success
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<populate watchlist: known scanner + corp NAT egress IPs via a Sentinel watchlist join, not inline>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the CompromisedUser + SourceIP; geolocate SourceIP and check whether the success used MFA and from a known ASN/country. Inspect the failed-user set — many distinct users from one IP = spray, not a typo. 2) Contain: if SourceIP is foreign/unrecognized, force-disable the compromised admin/VPN account, kill active SSL-VPN tunnels, block the SourceIP at the edge, and rotate the credential. 3) Hunt: from that SourceIP/account pivot to post-auth config changes (new admin accounts, sslvpn user groups), jsconsole admin logins, and any config download — feed into the FortiBleed jsconsole and rogue-admin UCs.
let lookback = 7d;
let window = 1h;
let Failed = CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Activity has "login" and (EventOutcome in~ ("failure","failed") or Message has_any ("login failed","Login failed","authentication failed","ssl-login-fail"))
| summarize Failures = count(), TargetUsers = dcount(DestinationHostName) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, window);
let Success = CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Activity has "login" and (EventOutcome in~ ("success","succeeded") or Message has_any ("login successful","SSL tunnel established"))
| summarize Successes = count(), CompromisedUser = make_set(DestinationHostName, 20) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, window);
Failed
| where Failures >= 30   // 30 = empirical spray burst floor per source per hour
| join kind=inner Success on SourceIP, TimeGenerated
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, Failures, TargetUsers, Successes, CompromisedUser
| order by Failures desc
APPLICATION

| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("fortios","fortigate","fortiproxy","ftnt-fortigate","sslvpn-plain","forticlient_ems") by Authentication.src, Authentication.dest, Authentication.user, Authentication.action, _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| stats sum(eval(if(action="failure",count,0))) as failures, sum(eval(if(action="success",count,0))) as successes, dc(user) as targeted_users, values(eval(if(action="success",user,null()))) as compromised_user, values(dest) as dest by src, _time
| where failures >= 30 and successes >= 1
| sort - failures
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("fortios","fortigate","fortiproxy","ftnt-fortigate","sslvpn-plain","forticlient_ems") by Authentication.src, Authentication.dest, Authentication.user, Authentication.action, _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| stats sum(eval(if(action="failure",count,0))) as failures, sum(eval(if(action="success",count,0))) as successes, dc(user) as targeted_users, values(eval(if(action="success",user,null()))) as compromised_user, values(dest) as dest by src, _time
| where failures >= 30 and successes >= 1
| sort - failures
FortiGate jsconsole / loopback admin login (CVE-2024-55591 auth-bypass exploitation) AIExploitation High
Hunts the high-fidelity exploitation signature of CVE-2024-55591: administrative logins attributed to the 'jsconsole' interface and/or successful super-admin logins sourced from the device loopback/local IP — the artifact the Node.js websocket auth-bypass leaves when an unauthenticated attacker forges super_admin access on FortiOS/FortiProxy. Rationale: Uses the two corroborated CVE-2024-55591 exploitation artifacts — `ui=jsconsole` in the admin-login record (matched in CommonSecurityLog Message) and super-admin logins from the device loopback/local IP (CIM Authentication.src=127.0.0.1) — reported by Arctic Wolf, watchTowr ('I Am The Super_Admin Now') and Trustwave. Both are near-zero in benign FortiGate operation. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/ • https://labs.watchtowr.com/get-fortirekt-i-am-the-super_admin-now-fortios-authentication-bypass-cve-2024-55591/ • https://trustwave.com/en-us/resources/blogs/spiderlabs-blog/cve-2024-55591-fortinet-fortios-fortiproxy-zero-day
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001 T1556
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately running CLI commands through the FortiGate GUI 'CLI console' widget (also tagged jsconsole) — distinguish by source being a real admin IP, not loopback
  • Automation/orchestration tooling (Ansible/FortiManager) driving CLI via the local console
  • Internal penetration test replicating CVE-2024-55591
  • Health-check scripts hitting the management interface from a jump host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the jsconsole/loopback login corresponds to a real admin session — legitimate jsconsole use originates from an authenticated GUI session with a genuine admin SourceIP; exploitation shows loopback/local src and no preceding interactive auth. Check FortiOS version against the CVE-2024-55591 fixed builds. 2) Contain: isolate the device's management interface from the internet, disable/rotate all admin accounts, and capture the running + startup config for IR. 3) Hunt: enumerate admin accounts and sslvpn user groups created/modified after the first jsconsole login, look for `--userfrom`-style audit-record tampering, and any config download/exfil to chain with the rogue-admin and FortiBleed config-extraction UCs.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Message has "jsconsole"
| where Message has_any ("login","logged in","logged-in","admin")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceProduct, DeviceExternalID, SourceIP, AdminUser = SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, Activity, EventOutcome, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Authentication.dest) as dest from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.app IN ("fortios","fortigate","fortiproxy","ftnt-fortigate") (Authentication.src="127.0.0.1" OR Authentication.src="0.0.0.0" OR Authentication.src="::1") by Authentication.user, Authentication.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| `ctime(firstTime)` | `ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Authentication.dest) as dest from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.app IN ("fortios","fortigate","fortiproxy","ftnt-fortigate") (Authentication.src="127.0.0.1" OR Authentication.src="0.0.0.0" OR Authentication.src="::1") by Authentication.user, Authentication.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| `ctime(firstTime)` | `ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - firstTime
FortiGate rogue super_admin / SSL-VPN account creation following CVE-2024-55591 exploit AIInstallation High
Hunts post-exploitation persistence for the FortiBleed/CVE-2024-55591 chain: creation of new FortiGate administrator accounts (often random usernames) or new SSL-VPN local users / user groups via config changes. This is how attackers convert a one-shot auth bypass into durable, high-privilege access for offline-cracked credential re-use. Rationale: Targets the documented CVE-2024-55591 post-exploit actions — new admin accounts with random names, new SSL-VPN local users and groups — via Fortinet config-change logs (cfgpath system.admin / user.group) and the CIM Change datamodel (action=created, object_category=user). Account creation on an edge appliance is rare and tightly change-controlled, so FP is low. Corroborated by Arctic Wolf and Cyble. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/ • https://cyble.com/blog/cve-2024-55591-the-fortinet-flaw-putting-critical-systems-at-risk/
ATT&CKT1136 T1098 T1133
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Planned admin onboarding by the network team during a change window
  • FortiManager/automation pushing a config template that provisions admin or VPN users
  • Legitimate SSL-VPN user-group expansion during an access-request rollout
  • MSP/managed-SOC provisioning a monitoring admin account
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the ActorAdmin and SourceIP that created the new object; correlate against an authorized change ticket and verify the actor session was not a jsconsole/loopback exploit login. Flag random-looking usernames. 2) Contain: delete or disable the unauthorized admin/VPN account and group, terminate its sessions, and rotate credentials for every legitimate admin on the device. 3) Hunt: review whether the new account granted VPN access, established tunnels into internal networks, or downloaded the device config; pivot on its SourceIP across other edge devices to scope the FortiBleed campaign footprint.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Message has_any ("system.admin","user.local","user.group")
| where Message has_any ("super_admin","prof_admin","accprofile","sslvpn")
| where Message has_any ("Object attribute configured","Added","cfgattr","New","create")

FortiBleed MSSQL login-failure burst then success (internet-exposed SQL spraying) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the FortiBleed campaign's parallel targeting of internet-exposed MSSQL: a single client IP generating a burst of SQL Server login failures (error 18456) across one or many logins within a short window — the spray signature Unit 42 observed against MSSQL devices alongside Fortinet and Sophos. Rationale: Covers the article's explicit observation that the FortiBleed actors also targeted MSSQL devices. Pivots on SQL Server error 18456 (login failed) parsed for CLIENT IP and login name in Sentinel's Event table, with a Defender DeviceLogonEvents fallback for Windows-auth brute force against the SQL host and a CIM Authentication path for Splunk. Threshold-based, so framed as a burst detector. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/what-is-fortibleed/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1078
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Application/service account with a stale connection string hammering the DB after a password change
  • Linked-server or ETL job misconfigured with wrong credentials retrying in a tight loop
  • Monitoring agent (SCOM/SolarWinds) probing SQL with expired creds
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanner credential audit against the SQL instance
  • Developer load-test pointing at the wrong SQL host
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("sqlmonitor","svc-etl","svc-backup")   // tune to your known SQL service accounts
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve ClientIP — internal app server vs external/unknown. Inspect the targeted login set: many distinct logins from one IP = spray; a single service account = likely stale credential. Check for any 18454/successful login from the same ClientIP right after the burst. 2) Contain: if external, block the ClientIP at the firewall, confirm the SQL instance is not directly internet-exposed, and disable SQL-auth logins that were sprayed; enforce that MSSQL sits behind the VPN/jump box. 3) Hunt: if a success followed, review that login's subsequent activity (xp_cmdshell, new SQL logins, linked-server abuse) and pivot the ClientIP across Fortinet edge logs to tie it to the broader FortiBleed spraying infrastructure.
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "LogonFailed"
| where LogonType in ("Network","Batch")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize Failures = count(), TargetedAccounts = dcount(AccountName), Accounts = make_set(AccountName, 30), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by RemoteIP, DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 30m)
| where Failures >= 30   // 30 failed network logons / 30 min from one source = spray
| order by Failures desc
let lookback = 7d;
let window = 30m;
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Source == "MSSQLSERVER"
| where EventID == 18456   // SQL Server: Login failed
| extend LoginUser = extract(@"Login failed for user '([^']+)'", 1, RenderedDescription)
| extend ClientIP = extract(@"\[CLIENT: ([0-9A-Fa-f\.:]+)\]", 1, RenderedDescription)
| where isnotempty(ClientIP)
| summarize Failures = count(), TargetedLogins = dcount(LoginUser), Logins = make_set(LoginUser, 30) by ClientIP, Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, window)
| where Failures >= 30
| order by Failures desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |

references:

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |

Exploitation. Installation. Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound connection to CL-STA-1062 / TinyRCT C2 and tool-staging infrastructure · [LLM] SoftEther VPN / VNT tunneler masquerading as VMware vmtools.exe · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Password-protected RAR staging of data for exfiltration (-hp) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
TinyRCT backdoor masquerading as PerfWatson2.exe executing from %LOCALAPPDATA% AIInstallation High
Hunts the CL-STA-1062 TinyRCT .NET backdoor, which masquerades as Visual Studio's PerfWatson2.exe but enforces an environment check that it runs only from %LOCALAPPDATA%. Legitimate PerfWatson2.exe ships inside the Visual Studio install tree under Program Files, so any PerfWatson2.exe launching from AppData\Local is article-specific TinyRCT behaviour. Rationale: Uses the article's exact masquerade name PerfWatson2.exe plus TinyRCT's own self-imposed %LOCALAPPDATA% execution constraint; legitimate PerfWatson2 lives under Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio, making AppData\Local execution near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/08/taiwan-web-servers-breached-by-uat-7237.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1497.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer running a portable/extracted copy of Visual Studio components from a profile folder
  • Visual Studio installer caching PerfWatson2 in AppData during an update (rare, usually Program Files)
  • Security tooling copying the binary to AppData for analysis on an analyst workstation
  • EDR sandbox detonation copying the sample into LocalAppData
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Microsoft Visual Studio\" and not(FolderPath has @"\Microsoft Visual Studio\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 and confirm it is not the signed Microsoft PerfWatson2 (legit is signed 'Microsoft Corporation' under Program Files). Check the parent process and whether the host concurrently beaconed to 45.32.113.172 or 139.180.134.221. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and quarantine the AppData\Local copy; block both C2 IPs at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: search the environment for any PerfWatson2.exe outside Program Files, for the GoogleUpdater scheduled task, and for choice.exe-based self-delete batch chains indicating TinyRCT cleanup.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "PerfWatson2.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\PerfWatson2.exe"
| where NewProcessName has @"\AppData\Local\"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound connection to CL-STA-1062 / TinyRCT C2 and tool-staging infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host connecting to the two confirmed CL-STA-1062 IPs: 45.32.113.172 (TinyRCT HTTP C2, ~10s beacon) and 139.180.134.221 (payload/tool-staging server hosting the PerfWatson2.exe backdoor and RAR tool archives). Pure-IOC network detection for both beaconing and payload pull. Rationale: Both IPs are explicitly named in the article (139.180.134.221 hosting PerfWatson2.exe; 45.32.113.172 as TinyRCT C2 in the kill-chain block) and confirmed across the Unit 42 report and Talos UAT-7237 overlap; raw IOC hits are high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher or sandbox sandboxing the sample and reaching the C2
  • Threat-intel scanning/validation services probing the IPs from a corporate range
  • Shared Vultr/cloud hosting reassigning the IP to a benign tenant after takedown (verify timestamps against report publication)
  • Internal vuln scanner configured to crawl flagged IOCs
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process; if it is PerfWatson2.exe, a fake vmtools.exe, or curl.exe from a web-server context, treat as confirmed. Note beacon cadence (~10s = TinyRCT). 2) Contain: block both IPs at firewall/proxy, isolate the source host, and capture memory before reboot. 3) Hunt: pivot on src_ip for prior 139.180.134.221 downloads (RAR/SoftEther tool pulls), and sweep all hosts for second-stage payloads delivered from the staging server.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.32.113.172", "139.180.134.221")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("45.32.113.172", "139.180.134.221")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SoftEther VPN / VNT tunneler masquerading as VMware vmtools.exe AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts CL-STA-1062's habit of disguising tunneling tools (SoftEther VPN, VNT) as VMware system binaries such as vmtools.exe. Flags processes named vmtools/vmtoolsd whose signing company is not 'VMware, Inc.' or whose product string references SoftEther — i.e. a VMware-named binary that isn't VMware. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's Figure 6/7 masquerade (SoftEther disguised as vmtools.exe, VNT disguised as a VMware executable); the company-name/path mismatch separates the tunneler from genuine VMware Tools without needing a hash. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/08/taiwan-web-servers-breached-by-uat-7237.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine VMware Tools where version metadata is stripped/empty after repackaging by an MSP
  • Older VMware Tools builds signed under a legacy company string ('VMware, Inc.' variations)
  • Third-party VM management tools legitimately named vmtools running from a non-standard path
  • Software-distribution systems staging VMware Tools in a temp folder before install
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has @"\VMware\VMware Tools\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the binary's digital signature and the command line for SoftEther/VNT tunnel arguments (server address, listen port). Confirm it isn't VMware-signed. 2) Contain: terminate the tunneler, isolate the host, and block its configured remote VPN/relay endpoint. 3) Hunt: look for scheduled tasks launching the same disguised binary, RDP sessions riding the tunnel, and the same masquerade name on peer hosts indicating lateral spread.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("vmtools.exe", "vmtoolsd.exe")
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "VMware, Inc." or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "SoftEther"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("vmtools.exe", "vmtoolsd.exe")
| where ActingProcessFileCompany != "VMware, Inc." or ActingProcessFileProduct has "SoftEther"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessFileCompany, ActingProcessFileProduct, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Scheduled task persistence for GoogleUpdater or VMware-disguised VNT binary AIInstallation Medium
Detects CL-STA-1062 establishing persistence via schtasks.exe creating a task named GoogleUpdater (TinyRCT loader) or a task launching a tunneler disguised as vmtools/VNT (Figure 7). Pivots on the task-creation command line rather than the binary itself. Rationale: Combines the article/kill-chain GoogleUpdater task name (TinyRCT loader) with the Figure 7 VNT-as-VMware scheduled task; task creation referencing these masquerade tokens is far more specific than generic schtasks alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Google Chrome/Updater creating GoogleUpdateTaskMachineCore tasks (note: name differs from 'GoogleUpdater')
  • VMware Tools installer registering a legitimate vmtools-related task
  • Admin scripts re-creating VMware service tasks during template provisioning
  • Software-packaging tools that template task names containing 'vmtools'
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "GoogleUpdateTaskMachine" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\VMware\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the full task action (the binary path and arguments the task launches) and verify whether it points to a signed Google/VMware binary in its standard location. 2) Contain: delete the malicious task, isolate the host, and quarantine the referenced binary. 3) Hunt: enumerate all scheduled tasks across the fleet for the same name/binary, and correlate the task creator process — if it was a web shell (w3wp.exe) or PerfWatson2.exe, escalate to full IR.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("GoogleUpdater", "vmtools", "VNT")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where CommandLine has_any ("GoogleUpdater", "vmtools", "VNT")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

IIS web shell (w3wp.exe) spawning recon, curl exfil, or RAR staging AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the CL-STA-1062 ASPX web-shell command-execution channel where the IIS worker process w3wp.exe spawns cmd/curl/rar and native recon binaries — the actor piped system/network enumeration to actor IPs via curl and staged source code into RAR archives directly from the web shell. Rationale: Encodes the article's web-shell-as-execution-mechanism (Figure 4 curl enumeration, Figure 2 source-code archiving) via the w3wp.exe parent pivot — IIS workers should virtually never spawn curl, rar, tracert, or whoami. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/08/taiwan-web-servers-breached-by-uat-7237.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate web applications shelling out to net.exe/whoami for diagnostics
  • Application deployment scripts invoking cmd.exe under the app pool identity
  • Monitoring agents that run ipconfig/netstat from a web context
  • Developer health-check endpoints that exec systeminfo
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck", "\\Monitoring\\") and FileName in~ ("ipconfig.exe","netstat.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the child command lines — recon piped to curl targeting 45.32.113.172/139.180.134.221 or rar with -hp confirms malicious use; review IIS logs for the requesting URI and source IP (the web shell). 2) Contain: pull the offending .aspx file, isolate the web server, and reset the app-pool service account credentials. 3) Hunt: enumerate recently written/modified .aspx files in web roots, and pivot on the source IP across other internet-facing servers for the same web-shell pattern.
